title: Sampling Theorem
body:
**A signal containing no frequency above $B$ is completely determined by samples taken at any rate
$f_s > 2B$.** Not approximately determined: the continuous signal can be reconstructed exactly from
the discrete samples. $2B$ is the Nyquist rate, and $f_s/2$ is the Nyquist frequency, the highest
frequency a given sample rate can represent.

This is the theorem that makes digital audio, digital images, and digital anything possible. It says
that throwing away all but countably many instants of a [[Continuous]] signal loses **nothing**,
provided the signal was band-limited and you sampled fast enough.

## Why $2B$

Sampling multiplies the signal by a Dirac comb (see [[Dirac Delta Function]]). By the
[[Convolution Theorem]], multiplying in time convolves in frequency, so the spectrum gets copied
and repeated at intervals of $f_s$. If $f_s > 2B$ the copies sit side by side with a gap and the
original can be cut back out with a low-pass filter. If $f_s < 2B$ **the copies overlap**, the
overlapping parts add, and no filter can separate them again. That overlap is [[Aliasing]], and the
factor of two is because a real signal's spectrum is symmetric: it occupies $[-B, B]$, which is
$2B$ wide.

The corollary that matters in practice: you must **filter before you sample**, not after. An
anti-aliasing low-pass filter in front of the ADC removes what cannot be represented. Once the
samples exist the damage is unrecoverable.

## This is the theory behind COMP 2659's audio hardware

That course covered the hardware; this one covers why the hardware has the numbers it does.

| [[COMPUTING MACHINERY 2]] (2nd year, hardware) | MATH 4199 (4th year, theory) |
|---|---|
| An ADC samples the waveform, see [[DAC's and ADC's]] | This theorem says how fast it must sample |
| [[Fidelity]] is lost at low [[Sample Rate]] | [[Aliasing]] is the mechanism of that loss |
| [[PCM]] stores [[Amplitude]] once per sample | The Dirac comb is the idealised model of that |
| [[Digital]] means [[Discrete]] values | Discretising costs nothing if $f_s > 2B$ |

CD audio samples at 44.1 kHz because human hearing tops out near 20 kHz, and $2 \times 20 = 40$,
plus headroom for the filter. That number is this theorem, and nothing else.

## Related

- [[Fourier Transform]], which is where "contains no frequency above $B$" is defined.
- [[Discrete Fourier Transform]] is what you run on the samples once you have them.
